newsitem.title: GREECE: GREECE BLASTS EU PARTNERS OVER CYPRUS.
newsitem.headline: GREECE BLASTS EU PARTNERS OVER CYPRUS.

text.p: Greece blasted its European Union partners on Tuesday and threatened it would block further EU enlargement if talks to admit Cyprus did not start as scheduled this year with the Greek-Cypriot side doing the negotiations.
Athens is angry by a push by the other 14 EU members away from a previous agreement that Cyprus's membership could be limited to its southern Greek part.
EU foreign ministers said after a meeting in Brussels on Monday that the northern Turkish-occupied third of Cyprus should also be involved in the process of admitting the island to the bloc.
"The path to EU enlargement to the east will become very difficult if the agreement concerning Cyprus' accession changes," government spokesman Dimitris Reppas told reporters.

"This (including Turkish-Cypriots in the talks) is a new development which is not acceptable by Athens. The EU's previous position which was adopted by all 15 members is stronger than any talks to change it," he added.
Foreign Minister Theodoros Pangalos described the EU's new position, spearheaded by Britain and Germany, as "hostile and deceitful" and said Greece would "not accept any lords" within the EU.

Diplomats in Brussels said that the strong stance by Greece's 14 EU partners was to pressure Athens to negotiate a settlement to the divided island, of which Turkey invaded the northern third in 1974, in response to a brief Greek Cypriot coup in Nicosia that was backed by Athens.

"The accession of a divided island would create serious problems to the EU and this is not a path that we or our partners are willing to take," British Foreign Secretary Malcolm Rifkind said in an interview with the Athens daily Ta Nea, published on Tuesday.
"This is why it is so important for both sides to work and find a solution taking advantage of the historic opportunity which the start of (Cyprus') accession talks offer," he added.
Talks on Cyprus' accession are scheduled to start six months after the EU concludes its ongoing intergovernmental review of its workings.
The international community, with the exception of Turkey, recognises the Greek Cypriot adminstration as the island's only legal government.
The EU and Washington have also put pressure on Athens and Ankara to find a formula and ease tensions over territorial differences in the Aegean Sea.

The two NATO allies came close to war over an uninhabited islet in the Aegean last year and Greece has approved a $12 billion arms programme for the next four years saying it will not negotiate its territory.
